title: Chapter 7 Mastery Quiz: Complex Factorial Designs & Quasi-Experiments
description: Master factorial matrices, main effects vs. interactions, quasi-experimental controls, and small-N reversal designs.

questions.question: What is the defining characteristic of a Factorial Experimental Design?

options.text: It includes two or more independent variables (factors)
It has exactly one independent variable and ten dependent variables
It does not require statistical analysis
It can only be used in naturalistic field observation

questions.explanation: A factorial design studies two or more independent variables simultaneously, testing all possible combinations of their levels.

questions.question: In standard psychological notation, how many Independent Variables and total experimental conditions are present in a 2 x 3 factorial design?

options.text: 2 IVs and 6 total conditions
3 IVs and 5 total conditions
5 IVs and 6 total conditions
2 IVs and 5 total conditions

questions.explanation: There are two numbers (2 IVs); the first IV has 2 levels and the second IV has 3 levels, yielding 2 x 3 = 6 unique conditions.

questions.question: What is a 'Main Effect' in a factorial experiment?

options.text: The overall effect of one independent variable on the dependent variable, averaged across all levels of the other independent variable
The effect of the confounding variable on the study outcome
The personal opinion of the lead investigator
The statistical power of a t-test

questions.explanation: A main effect represents the isolated impact of a single factor on the DV, collapsed across all levels of the other factors.

questions.question: What does an 'Interaction Effect' signify in a two-way factorial design?

options.text: The effect of one independent variable on the dependent variable changes depending on the level of the second independent variable
Participants talking to one another in the waiting room
The correlation between two demographic variables
The experimenter shaking hands with the participant

questions.explanation: An interaction occurs when the causal impact of Factor A depends on or is moderated by the specific level of Factor B.

questions.question: When plotting cell means on a line graph, what visual evidence strongly suggests that NO interaction is present?

options.text: The lines are parallel to one another
The lines cross in a giant X
The lines diverge steeply
One line is horizontal and the other line is vertical

questions.explanation: Parallel lines show that the effect of Factor A is constant across all levels of Factor B, indicating the absence of an interaction.

questions.question: What is a 'Crossover Interaction'?

options.text: An interaction where the lines on a factorial plot intersect, indicating that the effect of one IV completely reverses direction across levels of the other IV
When participants switch rooms during an experiment
When a study is published in two different journals
When an experimenter uses two different computers

questions.explanation: In a crossover interaction, the lines cross each other, showing that an IV has opposite effects depending on the level of another factor.

questions.question: Why must researchers be cautious when interpreting main effects when a significant interaction is present?

options.text: Because the interaction qualifies the main effect; the overall average may be misleading if the effect is only true in one specific condition
Because statistical software automatically deletes main effects when an interaction occurs
Because an interaction proves that the sample size was too small
Because the Belmont Report forbids reporting both simultaneously

questions.explanation: Interactions supersede main effects: broad averages hide the fact that the IV only works (or works in reverse) under specific conditions.

questions.question: What is a Mixed Factorial Design?

options.text: A design where at least one independent variable is between-subjects and at least one independent variable is within-subjects (repeated measures)
A design that combines humans and animals in the same cage
A study that mixes English and Spanish questions
An experiment with no control group

questions.explanation: A mixed factorial design incorporates at least one independent groups factor and at least one repeated measures factor.

questions.question: How many total conditions exist in a 2 x 2 x 3 factorial design?

options.text: 7 conditions
12 conditions (2 x 2 x 3 = 12)
8 conditions
24 conditions

questions.explanation: Multiplying the levels of each factor gives the total number of cells: 2 x 2 x 3 = 12 conditions.

questions.question: What is the key limitation that separates Quasi-Experiments from True Experiments?

options.text: Quasi-experiments lack random assignment of participants to experimental conditions
Quasi-experiments never collect quantitative data
Quasi-experiments are not recognized as scientific by peer-reviewed journals
Quasi-experiments do not require ethical approval

questions.explanation: Because participants in quasi-experiments cannot be randomly assigned, pre-existing selection biases threaten internal validity.

questions.question: In a Nonequivalent Control Group Pretest-Posttest design, why is administering a pretest essential?

options.text: To verify whether the non-randomized groups were equivalent on the dependent variable prior to the intervention
To artificially inflate statistical power to 1.00
To convert the study into a randomized controlled trial
To avoid having to compute posttest scores

questions.explanation: A pretest allows researchers to assess whether intact groups differed systematically before the treatment began.

questions.question: A state government introduces a new highway speed limit law. Traffic researchers track monthly road fatality rates for 24 months before and 24 months after the policy takes effect. What design is this?

options.text: Interrupted Time-Series Design
Single-case ABAB reversal design
Cross-sectional survey
Double-blind clinical drug trial

questions.explanation: Repeated continuous observations before and after an abrupt environmental or policy intervention represent an interrupted time-series design.

questions.question: What is the primary threat to an interrupted time-series design?

options.text: A simultaneous historical event occurring at the exact same time as the intervention
Random assignment error
Failure to calculate Cronbach's alpha
Participants taking too many surveys

questions.explanation: If another major event occurred at the exact same moment as the policy change, that historical event could account for the change in the dependent variable.

questions.question: How does adding a 'Nonequivalent Comparison Group' strengthen an interrupted time-series design?

options.text: It helps rule out historical events: if the fatality drop occurs only in the state with the law change and not in neighboring states, the law is the cause
It eliminates all speed limits
It makes the study completely double-blind
It changes the measurement scale to ratio

questions.explanation: A comparison group exposed to the same regional historical events provides a baseline, proving the effect was specific to the intervention.

questions.question: What distinguishes Small-N (Single-Case) Experimental Designs from classic observational case studies?

options.text: Single-case experiments systematically manipulate an independent variable and continuously measure outcomes across structured phases
Single-case experiments never study humans
Case studies use statistics, while single-case experiments do not
There is no difference; they are exact synonyms

questions.explanation: Single-case experiments possess experimental control: an independent variable is introduced, withdrawn, or staggered to demonstrate causal functional relations.

questions.question: In an ABAB single-case reversal design, what happens during the second 'A' phase?

options.text: The treatment is temporarily withdrawn (reversal to baseline conditions)
The participant is given double the medication dose
A new participant is brought into the room
The study is published immediately

questions.explanation: Phase A2 withdraws the treatment to demonstrate that the behavior returns toward baseline levels when the intervention is absent.

questions.question: Why is an ABAB reversal design considered one of the strongest demonstrations of causal control in behavioral science?

options.text: Because it demonstrates that the behavior changes if and only if the treatment is introduced, withdrawn, and reintroduced
Because it costs more money than a between-subjects trial
Because it requires over 1,000 subjects
Because it relies purely on subjective intuition

questions.explanation: Showing repeated functional replication across on-off-on phases provides overwhelming proof that the treatment—not coincidental history—causes the behavioral change.

questions.question: When can an ABAB reversal design NOT be used to evaluate a behavioral intervention?

options.text: When the intervention teaches a permanent skill (e.g., reading) that cannot be unlearned upon withdrawal
When the participant is an adult
When data are collected on a computer
When the baseline exceeds 10 days

questions.explanation: If a skill or insight is irreversible once acquired, withdrawing the intervention will not cause behavior to return to baseline, invalidating the reversal.

questions.question: What is the primary design structure of a Multiple-Baseline Design?

options.text: Treatment is introduced at staggered, different points in time across multiple behaviors, participants, or settings
Every participant receives three different medications simultaneously
The researcher takes baseline data in three different countries at once
The study combines qualitative and quantitative surveys

questions.explanation: Multiple-baseline designs stagger the start of treatment across different targets; showing that each target changes only when treatment begins proves causality without reversal.

questions.question: In a Multiple-Baseline Across Behaviors design, what should happen to Behavior 2 while Behavior 1 is receiving treatment?

options.text: Behavior 2 should remain at its stable baseline rate until treatment is specifically applied to it
Behavior 2 should immediately drop to zero
Behavior 2 should be deleted from the study
Behavior 2 should increase tenfold

questions.explanation: If untreated behaviors remain stable at baseline while only the treated behavior changes, experimental control is firmly confirmed.

questions.question: What statistical test is most commonly used to analyze data from a 2 x 2 between-subjects factorial experiment?

options.text: Two-Way Analysis of Variance (Two-Way ANOVA)
Independent samples t-test
Spearman rank correlation
Chi-Square goodness of fit

questions.explanation: A Two-Way ANOVA evaluates Main Effect A, Main Effect B, and the Interaction Effect (A x B) simultaneously.

questions.question: What is a 'Spreading Interaction' on a factorial plot?

options.text: An interaction where lines start together at one level of Factor B and diverge or fan out at the other level
When data points spill outside the boundaries of the paper
When participants talk about the study on social media
When standard deviations are zero

questions.explanation: A spreading interaction occurs when an IV has an effect under one condition (e.g., when a person is motivated) but virtually no effect under another condition.
